newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan warlord digs in against Taleban, front calm.
newsitem.headline: Afghan warlord digs in against Taleban, front calm.

text.p: Tanks, heavy artillery and multiple-launch Grad missiles of warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum were dug in at both ends of the vital Salang tunnel northwest of the Afghan capital Kabul on Wednesday.
However both the northern Uzbek leader's faction and the Islamic Taleban militia now in control of Kabul appeared keen to avoid a confrontation and no fighting was reported.

Colonel-General Chary, commander of Dostum's Jumbish-i-Milli frontline position, told reporters in what had the ring of a warning to the Taleban forces: "We don't want to fight but we will defend our territory."

Chary, speaking at his position overlooking the village of Olang, said Taleban forces were about three km (two miles) to the south. "We command the heights -- there has been no fighting here," he said.
Tanks, heavy artillery and Grad missile launchers could be seen at both ends of the strategically vital tunnel, around 70 km (45 miles) northwest of Kabul.
Taleban Acting Deputy Foreign Minister Sher Mohammed Stanakzai told reporters on Tuesday their forces did not want to fight Dostum.
The Taleban, who seized Kabul last Friday with barely a shot fired, are focusing on a perceived threat from former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.

Taleban-controlled Kabul Radio said on Wednesday their forces had entered the Panjsher Valley, Masood's stronghold, but said the front-line near the Salang tunnel between Taleban troops and those of Dostum was quiet.

The Taleban on Tuesday disowned an ultimatum sent by a Taleban commander to Dostum's forces the previous day, telling him to stand aside and let the Taleban cross the Salang pass over the formidable Hindu Kush mountain range.
The ultimatum was unauthorised and not valid, Stanakzai said.
"So far, we have no problem with Dostum and we hope this will be solved through negotiations. We don't want more fighting," he added. "We hope for a mutual understanding with Dostum."
Military experts said on Tuesday that Masood and Dostum may have to bury an old rivalry to confront the Taleban.
Dostum, a former defence minister, was involved in an attempt to seize Kabul in a military coup on January 1, 1994, setting off bloody fighting with Masood forces.
Aides to Masood at a secret location in the Panjsher Valley said on Tuesday that some contacts were continuing with Dostum, but indicated that the two men were far from reaching an agreement.
